names.name: wing
names.said: An order is counted, not weighed: six, ten, twenty, fifty. 'A dozen' means twelve pieces, not twelve wings.

etymology.root: Old Norse vængr → Middle English weng, winge → English wing; the food sense is a straight transfer from the bird's limb
etymology.note: On a menu the word slid from the whole limb to the pieces it gets cut into, so one wing off the bird sells as two or three wings. *Inference —* the counting unit followed the knife, not the bird.

text.what: A chicken's wing, and the pieces it becomes. Off the bird it runs drumette, flat and tip; a kitchen cuts it at both joints and usually throws the tip into stock, so what a menu calls a wing is one of two pieces. Order twenty and twenty pieces arrive, roughly ten birds' worth of one wing each.
text.how: Say the number, then the sauce, then bone-in or boneless, then the dip. A counter that asks 'flats or drums?' is offering something most places will not.

kin.as: The upper piece, the one that looks like a small drumstick.
The middle piece, two bones and the most skin.
The pointed end, usually cut off and boiled for stock.
Where the knife goes, and why a wing sells as two.
What a grocery calls the drumette and the flat when it sells them already split.
Sold under this word, cut from the breast, and argued about in court.

etymology.note: the Old Norse chain is general etymology; the menu sense is described, not dated
